I have farmed cotton in Quzhou for forty years, and I learned long ago that this soil gives back only what you put into it. Last year my 12 mu produced about 330 kg of seed cotton per mu, which was decent, but the bolls in the east half of the field were undersized because I cut the potassium back to save money, and a dry July stressed the plants because I only irrigated twice. This year I am targeting 340 kg per mu, and I will spend what I need to get there.

I start my fertilizer plan from the numbers. To produce 340 kg of seed cotton, the plants need to pull a lot of nutrients out of the ground, and Quzhou soil does not replenish itself. I will apply 22 kg of nitrogen per mu in total: I put down about 12 kg as base fertilizer before sowing—mixing compound fertilizer and urea into the soil—then top-dress another 10 kg of urea at flowering and early boll stage. I never dump all the nitrogen at once; the stalks will grow too tall, lodge, and drop bolls. For phosphorus, it all goes down at planting, 8 kg per mu as base, because cotton needs strong roots early if it is going to carry a heavy boll load. For potassium, I learned my lesson last year—this year it is 12 kg per mu, half at planting and half at first flowering. Potassium chloride is running about 4,000 yuan per ton now, which stings, but when I skimped last year I lost more than 20 kg of yield per mu, and at 7.5 yuan per kilogram for seed cotton that is over 150 yuan per mu gone. The arithmetic is simple.

I plant an improved Bt variety, not a hybrid. The seed costs me around 55 yuan per mu, but I save on sprays. Still, I will make 6 insecticide applications this season: one right after emergence for aphids, two in July for red spider mite and bollworm backup, and three more from late July through August for whitefly and any secondary pests that break through. Even Bt cotton needs protection when the pressure builds.

For water, my well has good fresh water—not like the salty wells some villages still struggle with—so I will irrigate three times: once before sowing to bank soil moisture, once at peak flowering in mid-July, and once in early August for boll filling. Pumping costs diesel, but one missed irrigation at flowering can cost 50 kg of yield.

I hire a tractor for rotary tillage at 45 yuan per mu. It breaks the clods fine and gives me a level bed for plastic mulch, which I lay to warm the soil and hold down weeds. My neighbor tried no-till last year and got patchy emergence; I will stick with what works.

My household is just my wife and me, so when picking season comes I will hire four laborers for about ten days. That cost is already in my head. Everything connects: if I spend 120 yuan more per mu on fertilizer, water, and sprays, I need at least 18 kg of extra yield to break even. I am certain I will get it, because I have watched the best-managed fields in my village, and I have done the calculation myself.
